reader.title: Reported lynching of Mark Dorlon
bases: Both items relay Robert Eaton's report that Dorlon was "lynched" in Arizona, for horse-stealing (A1) and by "Cowboys" (A2).

Eaton's secondhand report says Dorlon was lynched for horse-stealing (A1) by "Cowboys" (A2), which meets the definition if true; but the death is hearsay, no number of lynchers is given, and no date, place or confirming report appears (A1, A2).
Both items rest on the same informant, Robert Eaton, who himself only heard the news while in a Buffalo hospital (A1, A2); no Arizona or independent report was found.

summary.text: The reported lynching of Mark Dorlon was a killing of a Brooklyn youth in Arizona in 1888, known only from the account of a companion, Robert Eaton, who returned to Brooklyn that December.
Eaton said Dorlon had been lynched for horse-stealing by "Cowboys," but he had only heard the news secondhand, and no date, place or confirmation appeared in the coverage.
Dorlon, Eaton and George Strong were three Brooklyn boys who left home in search of adventure in the West, in February according to the Baltimore Deutsche Correspondent.
That paper said they set out with knives, rifles and cartridges intending to fight Indians, were caught by a blizzard in Chicago, and sold their weapons for lack of money in Omaha.
In Dakota a "Cowboy" took Dorlon in, while Strong and Eaton went on without him.
After the boys separated, Strong enlisted in the army "to escape starvation," and Eaton traveled with a circus through Nebraska, Colorado and Arizona before falling ill with typhus in Buffalo.
According to the German-language account, Eaton claimed that while in a Buffalo hospital he received word that Dorlon had been lynched in Arizona by "Cowboys."
The New-York Tribune gave the reason as horse-stealing.
Neither item names the place, the date, the number of lynchers or the manner of death, and neither gives Dorlon's race.
No report of an inquest, arrests or a confirmation of Dorlon's death was found in the coverage.

The New-York Tribune carried the story on December 19, 1888, as a single paragraph in its Brooklyn column "Gathered About the Town," between notes on the Raymond Street Jail and a suicide at a sugar refinery.
It stated Eaton's report flatly, as what he "reports," without comment.

Der Deutsche Correspondent of Baltimore ran a longer version on December 28 among its "Tagesneuigkeiten" (news of the day), told in a mocking tone that cast the boys' plan to fight Indians as a bloodbath happily averted when they had to sell their guns.

That paper marked the lynching as Eaton's own claim, writing that he "will" (claims to) have received the news, and it closed by saying he had come home "um viele Erfahrungen reicher" (richer by many experiences).

accounts.gist: Eaton claims he learned in a Buffalo hospital that Dorlon had been lynched in Arizona by "Cowboys"; the paper frames the claim with "will ... erhalten haben" (claims to have received).

framing.detail: A one-paragraph item under "Gathered About the Town" that passes on Eaton's report without comment.
A longer, mocking account of boys who went west "die Indianer zu befehden" (to fight the Indians), with the lynching given as Eaton's unverified claim.
